```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 10, fig.height = 6, dpi = 110,
                      comment = "#>")
options(width = 100)
```

*Experimental.* `stability_landscape()`, `landscape_trend()` and
`landscape_surface()` are new in Nestimate 1.0.1; their arguments and
output may change in later releases.

Which engagement states hold students, how long does it take to move
between them, and how stable is each student's own sequence? This article
answers these questions with Nestimate (Saqr, López-Pernas, & Misiejuk,
2026) for the states of a whole cohort, for groups of students with
different trajectories, over the program, and for each student.

The questions come from longitudinal research on student engagement. Saqr
and López-Pernas (2021) followed the engagement state of students in every
course of a full program and found trajectories that stayed engaged,
stayed in between, or were troubled; Saqr, López-Pernas, Jovanović and
Gašević (2023) traced the trajectories of students' online tactics and
strategies in the same way. A single snapshot of engagement does not
forecast achievement, while sustained engagement marks a stable academic
trajectory (Saqr, López-Pernas, Helske, & Hrastinski, 2023). López-Pernas
and Saqr (2024a) read the same dynamics as properties of a complex system,
the momentum of achievement and the inertia of disengagement, and Vemuri et
al. (2026) traced how disengagement persists among first-year students.

In the complex-systems view of these studies (Saqr, Schreuder, &
López-Pernas, 2024; Saqr, Dever, et al., 2025), a stable state is an
attractor that holds students and draws them back, and a stable student is
one whose sequence stays in few states for long spells (Saqr, López-Pernas,
& Tikka, 2026). A stable average can hide change within students
(López-Pernas, Conde, Raspopović Milić, & Saqr, 2026), so stability is
measured here for the states and for each student.

| Question | Function |
|----------|----------|
| How long do students stay in each state, and where do they go when they leave? | `stability_landscape()` |
| What are the persistence, return and sojourn times of each state? | `markov_stability()` |
| How long does it take to reach one state from another? | `passage_time()` |
| Is the chain one connected process? | `chain_structure()` |
| Do groups of students live in different landscapes? | `stability_landscape()` on a grouped network |
| Does the stability of each state change over the program? | `landscape_trend()` |
| Which state holds the students whose sequences are most stable? | `landscape_surface()` |
| How stable is each student's sequence? | `sequence_metrics()` |

## Data

`trajectories` records the engagement state of 138 students in each of 15
consecutive courses, coded with the three engagement states of Saqr and
López-Pernas (2021): `Disengaged`, `Average` or `Active`. A missing value
marks a course the student did not take; most missing values are trailing
runs, students who left the program.

```{r data}
library(Nestimate)
head(trajectories, 3)
```

The transition network (Saqr, López-Pernas, Törmänen, et al., 2025; Saqr,
López-Pernas, & Tikka, 2025) gives the probability of each state in the
next course given the state in the current one. The three states have a
natural order, and the landscapes are drawn in it.

```{r network}
network <- build_network(trajectories, method = "relative")
network
engagement <- c("Disengaged", "Average", "Active")
```

Active students stay Active with probability 0.70, Average students stay
Average with 0.61, and Disengaged students stay Disengaged with 0.48; a
Disengaged student moves to Average more often (0.40) than to Active
(0.12).

# The states

## How long do students stay in each state?

`stability_landscape()` draws the network as a ball in a set of cups
(Scheffer et al., 2009), the basins of attraction of the complex-systems
reading of engagement (López-Pernas & Saqr, 2024a; Saqr, López-Pernas, &
Tikka, 2026). The warning signals that precede a shift between basins have
been traced in students' engagement long before drop-out (Saqr,
López-Pernas, Tikka, & Spitzer, 2026). A state that is followed by itself
with probability $P_{ii}$ is left after $1 / (1 - P_{ii})$ courses on
average, its expected stay, and the depth of its cup is the log of that
stay, $-\log(1 - P_{ii})$. Expected stay is then $e^{\text{depth}}$, the
escape-time law of a particle in a potential well (Kramers, 1940); a state
that is always left at once has depth 0. The intervals come from 1,000
resamples of students.

```{r landscape}
landscape <- stability_landscape(network, states = engagement, iter = 1000,
                                 seed = 2026)
landscape
```

The table gives each cup's depth with its interval, the expected stay
(`dwell`), the stay probability and the share of observed courses spent in
the state. Active is the deepest cup (depth 1.20 [1.02, 1.38]): students
stay 3.3 courses on average once they are active. Average follows (0.94,
2.6 courses) and Disengaged is the shallowest (0.66, 1.9 courses). The
intervals of Active and Disengaged do not overlap. How deep a cup is and how
much time is spent in it are different things: Average holds 43% of the
courses against 38% for Active, because students enter Average more often,
but they leave it sooner.

With three states the chain also has a net circulation, the part of the
dynamics a landscape cannot show (Schnakenberg, 1976): 0.009 per course
[0.003, 0.016], running Active to Average to Disengaged and back to
Active. Students decline one step at a time and recover by the direct jump
more often than the reverse.

```{r landscape-plot, fig.height = 5}
plot(landscape)
```

The ball sits at the bottom of each cup; the grey bars are the 95%
intervals, and the right axis reads the depth as an expected stay. Under
each cup are its expected stay, its share of courses and where students go
when they leave it.

```{r landscape-exits}
summary(landscape, table = "exits")
```

Students who leave Disengaged go to Average three times as often as to
Active (0.40 against 0.12), and students who leave Active almost never
drop straight to Disengaged (0.035, 23 transitions in the whole data).
Re-engagement and disengagement both pass through Average.

## How stable is each state as a Markov chain?

`markov_stability()` reports the Markov quantities behind the landscape for
each state (Kemeny & Snell, 1976; Helske et al., 2024): persistence (the
probability of staying, $P_{ii}$), the stationary probability (the
long-run share of time in the state), the return time (the expected number
of steps to come back after leaving, $1/\pi_i$), the sojourn time (the
expected length of a stay, $1 / (1 - P_{ii})$), and the mean time to and
from the other states.

```{r markov-stability}
markov <- markov_stability(network)
markov
plot(markov)
```

The long run splits the time 0.44 Average, 0.37 Active and 0.19
Disengaged. Disengaged is the least visited state and the slowest to return
to (5.4 courses), and the other states are far from it: reaching
Disengaged takes 9.2 courses on average from the other two states, while
leaving it to reach them takes 4.5. Average is reached from the other
states in 3.2 courses.

## How long does it take to reach a state?

`passage_time()` gives the full matrix of mean first passage times: the
expected number of courses to reach the column state from the row state
for the first time (Kemeny & Snell, 1976). The diagonal is the return
time.

```{r passage}
passage <- passage_time(network, states = engagement)
passage
plot(passage)
```

A Disengaged student reaches Average in 2.8 courses and Active in 6.2. An
Active student reaches Disengaged only after 10.4 courses on average, the
longest passage in the matrix, and almost always through Average (8.0
courses from Average). Re-engagement from Disengaged is faster than
disengagement from Active. Saqr, López-Pernas and Tikka (2026) read this
asymmetry, slow decline and faster recovery, as resilience: the system
returns to its attractor more readily than it leaves it.

## Is the chain one connected process?

`chain_structure()` classifies the states of the chain: which states
communicate, which are recurrent or transient, whether any are absorbing,
and whether the chain is irreducible, aperiodic and reversible (Kemeny &
Snell, 1976). The stationary distribution and the passage times above
assume an irreducible chain.

```{r chain}
chain <- chain_structure(network)
chain
plot(chain)
```

The three states form one communicating class, so every state can be
reached from every other and nothing is absorbing. The chain is regular
(some power of the matrix is positive everywhere) and not reversible: the
flow from Active to Average to Disengaged and back to Active does not
balance its reverse, which is the circulation the landscape reported.

# Trajectory clusters

## Do the students follow distinct trajectories?

Engagement over a full program follows a small number of distinct
trajectories (Saqr & López-Pernas, 2021; Saqr, López-Pernas, Jovanović, &
Gašević, 2023). The VaSSTra method finds them by turning indicators into
states and clustering the sequences of states (López-Pernas & Saqr,
2024b). `build_clusters()` groups the sequences by their Hamming distance
with partitioning around medoids (Saqr, López-Pernas, Helske, et al.,
2024), here into three clusters.

```{r clusters}
clusters <- build_clusters(trajectories, k = 3, seed = 2026)
clusters
cluster_networks <- build_network(clusters)
state_distribution(cluster_networks)
```

The three clusters hold 47, 74 and 17 students, with an average silhouette
of 0.36, a moderate separation. Cluster 1 is mostly active (75% of its
observed courses), cluster 2 mostly average (60%, with 24% disengaged),
and cluster 3 mostly disengaged (80%). Cluster 3 also has little data: 70
observed courses for 17 students, out of 255 possible, because most of its
students left the program early.

```{r clusters-plot, fig.height = 7}
sequence_plot(clusters, type = "index", ncol = 3, nrow = 1)
```

Each row is one student and each column one course. Cluster 1 is mostly
Active and cluster 2 mostly Average, with runs of Disengaged; most rows of
cluster 3 end within the first courses, and the grey is the part of the
program those students did not take.

## What landscape does each cluster live in?

The same call on the grouped networks gives one landscape per cluster.

```{r cluster-landscape}
cluster_landscape <- stability_landscape(cluster_networks, states = engagement,
                                         iter = 1000, seed = 2026)
cluster_landscape
```

```{r cluster-landscape-plot, fig.height = 11}
plot(cluster_landscape)
```

The three clusters live in three different landscapes, each with one deep
cup.

- **Cluster 1** has its deep cup at Active (depth 1.63 [1.39, 1.89], 5.1
  courses per stay). Average and Disengaged are equally shallow (0.35 and
  0.39, under 1.5 courses per stay), and both drain towards Active: 62% of
  average courses and 47% of disengaged courses are followed by an active
  one. The net circulation is indistinguishable from zero (0.004
  [-0.004, 0.014]).
- **Cluster 2** has its deep cup at Average (1.12 [0.98, 1.25], 3.1 courses
  per stay). Active is as shallow as Disengaged (0.45 and 0.56), and 58% of
  active courses are followed by an average one. The circulation is clear
  of zero (0.014 [0.005, 0.024]).
- **Cluster 3** has its deep cup at Disengaged (2.20 [1.65, 2.74], 9.0
  courses per stay). Its other cups rest on very few transitions, 2 of them
  out of Active, so their intervals are wide: [0.00, 1.95] for Average and
  [0.00, Inf] for Active, an upper limit that is unbounded because Active is
  never left in some resamples.

## How long does it take to reach engagement in each cluster?

```{r cluster-passage}
passage_time(cluster_networks, states = engagement)
```

From Disengaged, a cluster 1 student reaches Active in 2.0 courses on
average, a cluster 2 student in 9.1 and a cluster 3 student in 44, far
beyond the 15 courses of the program. In the other direction, Active to
Disengaged takes 26.1 courses in cluster 1, 6.7 in cluster 2 and 2.0 in
cluster 3.

# The landscape across the program

## Does the stability of each state change over the program?

`landscape_trend()` estimates the cup depths in a sliding window of five
courses (courses 1-5, 2-6, ..., 11-15) and draws one line per state, with
intervals from resampling students across all windows at once.

```{r trend}
phase_trend <- landscape_trend(network, along = "phase", states = engagement,
                               iter = 500, seed = 2026)
phase_trend
```

```{r trend-plot, fig.height = 5}
plot(phase_trend)
```

The order of the cups holds over the whole program: Active is the deepest
in every window (between 1.03 and 1.32, a stay of about three courses),
Average is second and Disengaged the shallowest. Disengaged changes the
most: its depth falls from 0.72 in courses 1-5 to 0.42 in courses 6-10 and
rises to 1.01 in courses 10-14, so disengagement holds students longest
near the end of the program.

## Does it change differently in each cluster?

```{r cluster-trend, fig.height = 10}
cluster_trend <- landscape_trend(cluster_networks, along = "phase",
                                 states = engagement, iter = 500, seed = 2026)
cluster_trend
plot(cluster_trend)
```

In cluster 1, Active is the deep cup in every window (1.45 to 1.89), and
the Disengaged cup disappears over the program: from 0.69 in courses 1-5 to
0 in the last windows, where every disengaged course is followed by a
different state. In cluster 2, Average stays the deep cup and deepens at
the end (1.17 to 1.38), and Disengaged becomes stickier (0.53 to 0.86).
Cluster 3 runs out of data: its students leave the program, so its later
windows have no Average or Active courses, and in some windows its
Disengaged cup is never left (21 such points across the three clusters,
left out of the lines).

## How does the landscape itself move over the program?

The same windows, with the cups and ridges of the stationary distribution
(`depth = "occupancy"`), drawn as a 3D landscape: the states run across,
the program runs into the picture, and each cup becomes a channel. Here a
cup sits at $-\log \pi$, lower when students spend more of the window in
the state, and a ridge at $-\log$ of the probability flux between two
states, higher when the switch is rarer (Wang, Xu, & Wang, 2008). The
windows are six courses long.

```{r occupancy-surface, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 6.5}
occupancy_trend <- landscape_trend(network, along = "phase",
                                   depth = "occupancy", window = 6,
                                   states = engagement, iter = 500,
                                   seed = 2026)
occupancy_trend
plot(occupancy_trend, type = "surface")
```

For all students the landscape barely moves over the program. Average is
the lowest channel in every window (0.79 to 0.86), Active a little higher
(0.89 to 1.08) and Disengaged the highest (1.54 to 1.79).

```{r cluster-occupancy-surface, fig.width = 16, fig.height = 6}
cluster_occupancy <- landscape_trend(cluster_networks, along = "phase",
                                     depth = "occupancy", window = 6,
                                     states = engagement, iter = 500,
                                     seed = 2026)
cluster_occupancy
plot(cluster_occupancy, type = "surface")
```

The clusters' channels are steady too, but at different states. In
cluster 1 the Active channel stays low throughout (0.26 to 0.35) while the
Disengaged ground rises from 2.44 to 3.84: disengagement becomes rarer as
the program goes on. In cluster 2 the Average channel stays low (0.45 to
0.54) and Active stays high (1.76 to 2.09). Cluster 3 can be drawn only in
its first window: after that its students are disengaged or gone, and the
chain of a window has no stationary distribution.

# Landscapes across stability measures

## Which cup deepens as students become more stable?

`landscape_surface()` adds a second axis: a per-student stability measure
from `sequence_metrics()`. At each value of the measure it computes the cup
depths from the 30 students closest to that value, weighted by a tricube
kernel (Cleveland, 1979), so the surface runs from the most stable
students to the most volatile; the plot puts the most stable end in front.
Six measures are used: self-loop tendency (the share of courses that repeat
the previous state), longitudinal entropy, the complexity index, the
longest spell, cyclic feedback (how often a state recurs two or more
courses later) and initial-state persistence (the length of the opening
spell). The last section defines them.

```{r surface}
surface <- landscape_surface(network, states = engagement,
                             measure = c("self_loop_tendency",
                                         "longitudinal_entropy",
                                         "complexity_index",
                                         "max_spell_duration",
                                         "cyclic_feedback_strength",
                                         "initial_state_persistence"))
surface
```

```{r surface-plot, fig.width = 15, fig.height = 10}
plot(surface, ncol = 3)
```

Five of the six measures give the same answer. At the stable end every cup
deepens and Active is the deepest, between 2.94 and 3.19 on all five
measures, an expected stay of about 20 courses. Disengaged is the second
deepest for self-loop tendency, entropy and complexity (1.96 to 2.49, 7 to
12 courses): the most stable students are either stably active or, fewer
of them, stably disengaged. At the volatile end all three cups are shallow
and of similar depth (0.14 to 0.90). Cyclic feedback differs: as
recurrence rises, the Active cup deepens (0.63 to 1.23) and the Disengaged
cup becomes shallower (0.99 to 0.54).

The measures come from the same sequences as the depths, so the cups of the
most stable students are deep by construction, self-loop tendency most of
all, and the depths at the stable end exceed any stay the 15-course
program can show. What the surface adds is which cup deepens as stability
rises: Active first, Disengaged second.

## Does the same hold inside each cluster?

```{r cluster-surface}
cluster_surface <- landscape_surface(cluster_networks, states = engagement,
                                     measure = c("self_loop_tendency",
                                                 "longitudinal_entropy"))
cluster_surface
```

```{r cluster-surface-plot, fig.width = 11, fig.height = 14}
plot(cluster_surface)
```

Within clusters, stability deepens the cluster's own cup. In cluster 1 the
Active cup deepens from 0.91 for the students with the lowest self-loop
tendency to 2.86 for the highest, and it is the deepest cup at both ends
of both measures. In cluster 2 the Average cup deepens from 0.61 to 1.92:
the most stable cluster 2 students are stably average, not stably active.
Cluster 3 has 4 to 8 effective students per slice, so its surfaces show no
more than its deep Disengaged cup.

# The students

The network and the landscapes describe the states of a group, and a
group-level description can misrepresent the students in it (Saqr, 2024;
Saqr, Vogelsmeier, & López-Pernas, 2024); in self-regulated learning, the
average process does not reflect the process of individual students (Saqr
& López-Pernas, 2024). Saqr, López-Pernas and Tikka (2026) read stability
from each student's own sequence: a stable student visits few states, stays
long in each, returns to the same state, and spends most of the program in
one state that acts as their attractor. They group the sequence indices
into three families, diversity of states, resistance to change and
structural dynamics. `sequence_metrics()` computes the indices, as
`sequence_indices()` in codyna does (Tikka, López-Pernas, & Saqr, 2026);
most are also defined in TraMineR (Gabadinho et al., 2011). `indices`
selects the ones returned.

## How varied is each student's sequence?

The first family measures the diversity of states. `unique_states` counts
the distinct states a student visits. `longitudinal_entropy` is the
Shannon entropy of the student's state proportions $p_s$, divided by the
log of the number of states $S$ so that it runs from 0 to 1:
$-\sum_{s=1}^{S} p_s \log p_s / \log S$. `simpson_diversity` is the
probability that two courses drawn from the sequence are in different
states, $1 - \sum_{s=1}^{S} p_s^2$. Low values mean a sequence concentrated
in one state, the mark of a strong attractor (Saqr, López-Pernas, & Tikka,
2026).

```{r diversity}
diversity <- sequence_metrics(trajectories,
                              indices = c("valid_n", "unique_states",
                                          "longitudinal_entropy",
                                          "simpson_diversity"))
summary(diversity)
```

Two students have no observed course and get `NA` in every index, and 20
are observed for fewer than 15 courses: a sequence ends at its last
observed course. The typical student visits two of the three states. The
mean entropy is 0.56 and the mean Simpson diversity 0.38: the cohort is
more varied than the mostly engaged students Saqr, López-Pernas and Tikka
(2026) analysed (0.38 and 0.27).

```{r diversity-single}
subset(sequence_metrics(trajectories,
                        indices = c("first_state", "valid_n",
                                    "unique_states")),
       unique_states == 1)
```

The students who visit a single state are of two kinds. Five are Active in
all 15 courses: a single attractor that held for the whole program. Seven
are Disengaged and are observed for one or two courses only: their
sequences are stable because they ended, not because they resisted change.
A diversity of 0 needs `valid_n` beside it before it can be read as
stability.

## How strongly does each student resist change?

The second family measures resistance to change. `self_loop_tendency` is
the share of a student's transitions that stay in the same state and
`transition_rate` the share that change it; the two sum to 1.
`mean_spell_duration` and `max_spell_duration` are the mean and the longest
run of one state, in courses. `initial_state_persistence` is the length of
the opening spell as a share of the sequence, `initial_state_proportion`
the share of the sequence spent in the first state, and
`initial_state_influence_decay` the share of the first third spent in the
first state minus the share of the last third, positive when the first
state fades.

```{r resistance}
summary(sequence_metrics(trajectories,
                         indices = c("self_loop_tendency", "transition_rate",
                                     "mean_spell_duration",
                                     "max_spell_duration",
                                     "initial_state_persistence",
                                     "initial_state_proportion",
                                     "initial_state_influence_decay")))
```

Students repeat their state in 63% of transitions on average (median 57%,
range 21% to 100%), and change it in the other 37%. The median spell lasts
2.1 courses and the median longest spell 5 courses. The median opening
spell covers 13% of the sequence, two courses of fifteen, although the
first state takes 56% of the sequence on average, because students come
back to it. The mean influence decay is 0.17: for most students the first
state weakens over the program. The cohort resists change less than the
mostly engaged students of Saqr, López-Pernas and Tikka (2026), whose mean
self-loop tendency was 0.75 and initial-state persistence 0.45.

## Where does each student's sequence settle?

The third family describes the structure of a sequence.
`cyclic_feedback_strength` is the largest share, over lags of two or more
courses, of positions whose state recurs that many courses later.
`dominant_state` is the student's most frequent state, their attractor;
`dominant_proportion` its share of the sequence and `dominant_max_spell`
its longest spell. `transition_complexity` is the share of the six possible
changes of state that the student makes at least once. `emergent_state` is
a state that settles in later in the program and outlasts the opening.

```{r structure}
structure_indices <- sequence_metrics(trajectories,
                                      indices = c("dominant_state",
                                                  "dominant_proportion",
                                                  "dominant_max_spell",
                                                  "cyclic_feedback_strength",
                                                  "transition_complexity",
                                                  "emergent_state"))
summary(structure_indices)
```

The dominant state takes 71% of a student's sequence on average and never
less than 40%: every student has an attractor that holds at least two
courses in five. Students use a third of the possible changes (median 0.33,
two of six).

```{r attractors}
aggregate(cbind(self_loop_tendency, dominant_proportion,
                longitudinal_entropy, mean_spell_duration) ~ dominant_state,
          data = sequence_metrics(trajectories), FUN = median)
```

The attractors differ in how firmly they hold their students. Students
whose attractor is Active are the most stable: the median student repeats
their state in 67% of transitions, spends 73% of the program in Active and
stays 2.5 courses at a time. Students whose attractor is Average are the
least stable on three of the four indices; Disengaged students have the
shortest spells (2.0 courses). The deepest cup of the landscape, Active,
holds its individual students most firmly too.

## Do students end where they started?

A complex system is sensitive to its initial conditions (Saqr,
López-Pernas, & Tikka, 2026): the state a student starts in may shape the
state they end in.

```{r first-last}
first_last <- table(sequence_metrics(trajectories,
                                     indices = c("first_state",
                                                 "last_state")))
first_last
mosaic_plot(first_last, xlab = "First state", ylab = "Last state", seed = 1)
```

Half the students (70 of 136) end in the state they started in. The start
carries most at the extremes: 26 of the 52 students who start Active end
Active and only 5 end Disengaged, and 17 of the 34 who start Disengaged end
Disengaged and only 3 end Active. The mosaic marks these cells by their
standardised residuals: Active to Active and Disengaged to Disengaged occur
more often than independence predicts, and the crossings between the
extremes less often.

## How much of each sequence is spent in the favourable state?

`integrative_potential` weights each course by its position, so that time
in Active late in the program counts more than time in Active at the start
(Brzinsky-Fay, 2018); `favorable` names the favourable state.

```{r integrative}
summary(sequence_metrics(trajectories, favorable = "Active",
                         indices = c("integrative_potential",
                                     "complexity_index")))
```

The median student spends a position-weighted 22% of the program in Active
(mean 0.35), and a quarter of the students spend almost none. The
complexity index combines the families into one number per student:
$0.4 \times$ entropy $+ 0.4 \times$ transition rate $+ 0.2 \times$ the
coefficient of variation of the spell lengths (capped at 1), 0 for a
student who never changes state. Its mean is 0.50 (range 0 to 0.78);
built from entropy and the transition rate, it ranks the students much as
those two do.

# Related articles

The predictability of the process (transition entropy, whether the next
state depends on more than the current one, which histories change it) is
covered in the transition-entropy vignette and the higher-order network
article. The stability of the estimates (bootstrap, Bayesian certainty,
split-half reliability, case-dropping of edges and centralities) is
covered in the model assessment article.
